item.title: FMF signs 14-year-old Grace Khelan as ambassador, backs her 2028 Olympic dream
item.description: At just 14 years old, Grace Elizabeth Khelan is already setting her sights on the Olympic Games, with support from FMF helping to boost her journey in swimming. Khelan, who is a Year 9 student at Jai Narayan College, says swimming has been a childhood passion inspired by her siblings, who were also strong swimmers.
item.content:encoded:
At just 14 years old, Grace Elizabeth Khelan is already setting her sights on the Olympic Games, with support from FMF helping to boost her journey in swimming.

Khelan, who is a Year 9 student at Jai Narayan College, says swimming has been a childhood passion inspired by her siblings, who were also strong swimmers.

She says she progressed in the sport after discovering her own potential and became increasingly motivated to pursue swimming after learning about drowning cases in Fiji.

Khelan is now balancing swimming with paddling, running, gym sessions and her academic commitments.

She says despite the demanding schedule, she is able to manage both sport and school with the help of a strong support system including her parents, coach and family.

Khelan adds her typical day begins at 4am, followed by stretching and an early morning swimming session from 5.30am to 7am before heading to school.

She says after finishing classes at around 3.20pm, she returns to training, with additional swimming sessions scheduled throughout the week.

The 14-year-old says preparation for her Olympic ambition includes swimming, running, paddling and gym work, which she says is progressing well.

The young swimmer urges others to keep trying, training and to never give up.

Khelan's father Michael Khelan says to swim in the Olympics has been a dream for her daughter and the support from FMF is a great opportunity to fulfill that dream.

Meanwhile, FMF has signed a three-year contract with Khelan as its ambassador and will be supporting her in her bid for the 2028 Olympics.

item.title: Fiji’s first in-country trained gynaecological oncologist Dr Nanise Sikiti to share her story on fijivillage Her-Story
item.description: From studying under a kerosene lamp in Levuka to becoming Fiji’s first in-country trained gynaecological oncologist, Dr Nanise Sikiti’s journey is one of sacrifice, resilience and determination. Dr Sikiti will share her inspiring story on fijivillage Her-Story with Temalesi Vono on Wednesday at 7pm.
item.content:encoded:
From studying under a kerosene lamp in Levuka to becoming Fiji’s first in-country trained gynaecological oncologist, Dr Nanise Sikiti’s journey is one of sacrifice, resilience and determination.

Dr Sikiti will share her inspiring story on fijivillage Her-Story with Temalesi Vono on Wednesday at 7pm.

Dr Sikiti will share the beginning of her journey in humble surroundings in Levuka.

She will also speak about the sacrifices she has made throughout her career, the challenges of balancing family and professional responsibilities, and the people and experiences that have shaped the woman and doctor she is today.

You can watch fijivillage Her-Story on our facebook page, YouTube channel, and TikTok and X account, fijivillage at 7pm on Wednesday.

You can also catch the podcast, fijivillage Her-Story on Spotify and Apple Podcasts.

item.title: Leaders need to understand younger employees rather than viewing them as difficult - Nadakuitavuki
item.description: Leaders need to take the time to understand younger employees rather than simply viewing them as difficult to manage. Permanent Secretary for the Ministry of Information Eseta Nadakuitavuki highlighted this while answering a question during the Leadership Fiji Leaders Lounge “Voices of Leadership” session.
item.content:encoded:
Leaders need to take the time to understand younger employees rather than simply viewing them as difficult to manage.

Permanent Secretary for the Ministry of Information Eseta Nadakuitavuki highlighted this while answering a question during the Leadership Fiji Leaders Lounge “Voices of Leadership” session.

Nadakuitavuki says working with the younger generation can be a challenge, but only when leaders do not take the time to understand them.

She says the younger generation entering the workforce is fearless, has a mind of its own and is not afraid to express itself or pursue what it wants.

INSERT: PS on younger generation 8th Sept

Nadakuitavuki says some of the expectations younger people bring into the workplace can be difficult to manage, including, what she describes, a sense of entitlement.

She says this is something that can be traced back to how younger generations were raised, adding that her own experience as a mother has also helped her understand the changing expectations of younger people.

Meanwhile, Minister for Lands and Mineral Resources Filimoni Vosarogo says younger workers also bring strong technology skills into the workplace.

He says they have grown up and received their education in an environment where technology is part of everyday life.

He says younger employees can understand technology more easily and, in his experience, can produce work much faster.

He says there have been occasions when he expected a task to take a day or two, but a younger employee completed it within hours.

Vosarogo says while younger employees can be highly productive, leaders still need to understand and work with the challenges they face.

He says punctuality issues and accidents are some of the concerns he has encountered, but believes leaders should take time to understand employees before taking disciplinary action.

The Minister says he has sat down with employees facing serious workplace issues and worked through their expectations and problems.

Director and Co-Founder of Pacific Island Beverages Pte Limited Rajesh Patel says businesses also need to change their approach as the younger generation becomes a larger part of the workforce.

Patel says challenges such as absenteeism have always existed and should not simply be blamed on the new generation.

He says businesses need to ask themselves how they can adapt and introduce greater flexibility.

He says business leaders who have been doing things the same way for many years now need to change their approach.

Patel says there is no alternative for businesses because the younger generation is now part of the workforce.

He says businesses that are able to adapt to the changing workforce will be better positioned for success.

When asked what advice they would give young leaders who are still developing wisdom through experience, Vosarogo says young people should not rush the process of becoming a leader.

He says young leaders should serve their time, trust the process and use the opportunities they have now to develop the skills, values and principles they will need later.

Patel says mentoring and maintaining a strong connection with young employees is important.

He says while some younger employees may expect promotions soon after entering an organisation, leaders need to work closely with them, gain their trust and help them understand that career progression takes time.

He says organisations sometimes lose good people when leaders fail to stay connected with them.

He says leaders need to get closer to individuals and their teams, communicate with them and support their development so they can grow with the organisation.

Meanwhile, Nadakuitavuki’s advice to young people who are afraid to start is simple: “just do it”.

She says failure is part of the process and what matters is how people respond when they fail.

She says young people have a choice between getting back up and moving forward or remaining focused on their failure.

She says leadership is also about making choices, and young people should not allow the fear of failure to stop them from taking the first step.

item.title: St Joseph's alumni use reunion to mentor young women and promote women's leadership
item.description: The St Joseph's Secondary School Alumni are using their reunion to mentor young women and tackle important issues around women's leadership, law, governance and health. Alumni President Lavinia Kaumaitotoya highlighted this to fijivillage News saying this year's reunion is about more than getting together socially, with programmes designed to create meaningful conversations between different gener
item.content:encoded:
The St Joseph's Secondary School Alumni are using their reunion to mentor young women and tackle important issues around women's leadership, law, governance and health.

Alumni President Lavinia Kaumaitotoya highlighted this to fijivillage News saying this year's reunion is about more than getting together socially, with programmes designed to create meaningful conversations between different generations of alumnae.

Kaumaitotoya says a Law and Governance session was held at the Fiji Museum this morning, where four alumnae, including Lisa Apted and Imrana Jalal, shared their experiences and views.

She says discussions focused on how law and governance have shaped their work, protecting women, advocating for women's issues and pushing for greater women's leadership in the corporate world and other sectors.

Kaumaitotoya says the speakers shared valuable lessons and experiences that younger alumnae can learn from.

She says the session was organised by alumnae from the 1990s, and similar sessions are being held throughout the week to allow older and younger generations to learn from each other.

Kaumaitotoya says some of this week's programmes are specifically targeted at alumnae from the 2000s onwards as they try to create mentoring spaces for the younger generation.

She says the reunion is celebrating seven decades of women's sisterhood and leadership, but they cannot celebrate that achievement without also investing in women who are still developing as leaders.

Meanwhile, about 150 alumnae visited the State House today following an invitation from the President.

Kaumaitotoya says the visit is primarily for alumnae who have travelled from overseas, and the President is expected to continue discussions around today's theme of law and governance.

She says they are grateful that the country's leadership has recognised the alumni and provided them with the opportunity to visit the State House.

Insert: Kaumaitotoya on Sisterhood 8th Sept 26

The celebrations will continue tonight with Waimanu Road to the World at the St Joseph's Secondary School Hall.

Kaumaitotoya says alumnae will choose a country and wear attire representing that country, while those travelling from overseas will also have an opportunity to share aspects of where they are now living.

She says one alumna has travelled from Hong Kong specifically to be part of the reunion and celebrate their sisterhood.

Tonight's programme is being organised by alumnae from the 2010s to the present, giving younger members the opportunity to organise an event that reflects their generation.

The programme continues tomorrow morning with a health walk, where participants are being encouraged to wear their St Joseph's T-shirts.

This will be followed by a discussion led by alumnae working in the medical field on women's health and issues that can help women live longer and healthier lives.

item.title: Fiji passport services resume after technical issues resolved
item.description: The technical issues affecting the passport system have been resolved, and services have now resumed operating normally. The Fiji Immigration Department says members of the public can now access passport services.
item.content:encoded:
The technical issues affecting the passport system have been resolved, and services have now resumed operating normally.

The Fiji Immigration Department says members of the public can now access passport services.

They appreciate the patience and understanding during the temporary suspension of services and apologise for any inconvenience caused.

The earlier disruption led to frustration among members of the public who turned up at the Immigration office seeking services.
